etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English pilegrim, from Old French pelegrin, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner”). Doublet of peregrine.

The change of –r...r– to –l...r– is an effect of dissimilation in early Romance; compare Italian cognate pellegrino.

definitions.definition: One who travels, especially on a journey to visit sites of religious significance.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Hebrews 11:13:
quote.text: strangers and pilgrims on the earth
"I wouldn't unfork that horse yet, pilgrim. I want a good look at ya first."

definitions.definition: (historical) A silk screen formerly attached to the back of a woman's bonnet to protect the neck.
(intransitive) To journey; to wander; to ramble.

quote.citation: 1681, Nehemiah Grew, Musæum Regalis Societatis. Or A Catalogue & Description of the Natural and Artificial Rarities Belonging to the Royal Society and Preserved at Gresham Colledge. […], London:  […]  W. Rawlins, for the author, →OCLC:
quote.text: For that he hath no certain home, or diet, but pilgrims up and down every where, feeding upon all sorts of Plants

quote.citation: 1851, Thomas Carlyle, The Life of John Sterling:
quote.text: [T]o all galleries, churches, sistine chapels, ruins, coliseums, and artistic or dilettante shrines he zealously pilgrimed[.]
